phy_edx.13.0.summary: The **kinetic theory (particle model)** says that all matter is made of tiny **particles** that are always moving. The three **states of matter** (solid, liquid and gas) are explained by differences in how the particles are **arranged**, how they **move**, how strong the **forces between them** are and how much **energy** they have. Using this simple model you can explain the everyday properties of each state, such as why solids keep their shape, why liquids flow and why gases can be compressed and fill any container.

core.p: The particle model treats every substance as being made of huge numbers of tiny particles (atoms or molecules). The word **kinetic** means 'to do with movement': the key idea is that these particles are **always moving**, and the faster they move the more **kinetic energy** they have.
bullets: All matter is made of **particles** too small to see.
Particles are **always moving** (or vibrating), even in solids.
There are **forces of attraction** between particles; these are strongest when particles are close together.
Heating a substance gives its particles **more energy**, so they move faster.
The **state** of a substance depends on the balance between the particles' energy and the forces between them.

callouts.p: A model in which matter is made of tiny particles that are in constant motion, used to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.

core.h: Arrangement, movement and energy at a glance
core.p: Most exam questions on this point ask you to describe or compare the three states. Learn this table: it covers every property the mark schemes reward.
bullets: Compare states using the four headings: **arrangement**, **movement**, **forces**, **energy**.
Use comparative words: closer, further apart, faster, stronger, weaker.
Gases have the most energy; solids have the least (for the same substance).

core.p: In a solid the particles are held **very close together** in a **regular, fixed pattern** by **strong forces of attraction**. They cannot move from place to place, but they do **vibrate about fixed positions**.
bullets: Particles are touching and arranged in a **regular lattice**.
Particles **vibrate** about fixed positions; they do not swap places.
**Strong forces** hold each particle in position.
Particles have the **least kinetic energy** of the three states.
So a solid has a **fixed shape** and a **fixed volume**.
A solid **cannot be compressed** because there are no gaps between particles to squash into.
A solid **cannot flow** because the particles cannot move past each other.

callouts.p: Never write that particles in a solid are 'still' or 'not moving'. They vibrate about fixed positions.

core.p: In a liquid the particles are still **close together** (mostly touching) but are arranged **randomly**. The forces between them are **weaker than in a solid**, so particles can **move around and slide past each other**.
bullets: Particles are close together with **no regular pattern**.
Particles **move around** each other in random directions.
Forces of attraction are **weaker** than in a solid but still hold the particles together.
Particles have **more kinetic energy** than in the solid.
So a liquid has a **fixed volume** but **no fixed shape**: it takes the shape of its container.
A liquid can **flow** because particles can slide past each other.
A liquid is **very hard to compress** because the particles are already touching.

core.p: In a gas the particles are **far apart** with **large gaps** between them. The forces between them are **very weak**, so particles move **quickly** and **randomly** in all directions, in straight lines until they hit another particle or the container wall.
bullets: Particles are **far apart**: the gaps are much bigger than the particles themselves.
Particles move **rapidly** and **randomly** in all directions.
Forces between particles are **very weak** (often treated as negligible).
Particles have the **most kinetic energy** of the three states.
So a gas has **no fixed shape and no fixed volume**: it spreads out to **fill any container**.
A gas can **flow** and is **easily compressed** because particles can be pushed into the empty gaps.
Particles **collide** with each other and with the container walls.

callouts.p: In a gas the spaces between particles are large compared with the size of the particles; this explains why gases are easily compressed.

core.p: Whether a substance can be squashed depends on whether there is **empty space** between its particles. This is a favourite 'explain' question.
bullets: Gas: **large gaps** between particles, so pushing a piston moves particles closer together: the gas compresses.
Liquid: particles are **already touching**, so there is almost no space to squash into.
Solid: particles are touching in a fixed pattern, so it **cannot be compressed**.
This is why gases are used in car tyres and air cushions, and liquids are used in hydraulic brakes.

core.p: Whether a substance keeps its shape depends on whether its particles are **held in fixed positions** or are **free to move past each other**.
bullets: Solids: strong forces hold particles in **fixed positions**, so the shape cannot change unless a force breaks or bends it.
Liquids: particles can **slide past each other**, so the liquid flows and takes the shape of the bottom of its container.
Liquids keep a fixed volume because the forces still keep particles **close together**.
Gases: particles move freely and quickly in all directions, so a gas **spreads out** to fill the entire container.
Liquids and gases are both called **fluids** because they can flow.

callouts.p: For 'explain' questions, state the property AND the particle reason, for example: 'a liquid can flow because its particles can move past each other'.

core.h: Energy and temperature in the particle model
core.p: Particles in a substance have **kinetic energy** because they move. When a substance is **heated**, energy is transferred to the particles and they move or vibrate **faster**. The **temperature** of a substance is linked to the **average kinetic energy** of its particles.
bullets: Heating a solid makes its particles **vibrate more**.
Heating a liquid or gas makes its particles **move faster**.
Higher temperature means a higher **average kinetic energy** of particles.
Not all particles move at the same speed: there is a range of speeds; temperature relates to the **average**.
For the same substance: **gas particles have more energy than liquid particles**, which have more than solid particles.

callouts.p: Increasing the temperature increases the average kinetic energy (speed) of the particles.

core.h: Changing state in the particle model
core.p: The particle model also explains what happens when a substance changes state. Energy supplied by heating lets particles **overcome some of the forces** holding them together; removing energy lets the forces pull particles back together. The particles themselves do **not change**: only their arrangement and movement change.
bullets: **Melting** (solid to liquid): particles gain enough energy to break out of their fixed positions.
**Boiling / evaporating** (liquid to gas): particles gain enough energy to overcome the forces and move far apart.
**Condensing** (gas to liquid) and **freezing** (liquid to solid): energy is transferred away and forces pull particles closer.
**Sublimation**: a solid changes directly into a gas.
The particles are the **same particles** in every state: a change of state is a **physical change**.

callouts.t: Particles do not expand or melt
callouts.p: When ice melts, the water molecules themselves do not melt, get bigger or change. Only their arrangement, spacing and motion change.

core.p: Because particles in liquids and gases are **constantly moving randomly**, they gradually spread out and mix. This explains why a smell spreads across a room or a drop of ink spreads through water without stirring.
bullets: Particles move in **random directions** and collide with each other.
Over time they **spread out** from where there are many of them to where there are fewer.
Mixing is faster in **gases** than in liquids because gas particles move faster and have more space.
Diffusion is faster at **higher temperatures** because particles move faster.
Diffusion does not happen noticeably in solids because particles are fixed in position.

core.p: Particle diagrams are a **simplified model**. They are very useful for explaining properties, but they leave things out. Higher-level answers may ask you to evaluate the model.
bullets: Particles are drawn as **solid spheres**, but real atoms and molecules are not hard balls.
Diagrams are **2D**, but real substances are **3D**.
The **forces between particles** are not shown.
Gas particle diagrams usually show particles much **closer together** than they really are.
Diagrams cannot show **motion** well; arrows only hint at it.
All particles are drawn the **same size**, which is not true for mixtures.

callouts.p: Draw circles of equal size. Solid: regular rows touching. Liquid: mostly touching, random, filling the bottom of the box. Gas: few circles widely spaced. Never overlap circles.

analogy.p: A **solid** is like students sitting in an exam hall: in neat rows, close together, unable to leave their seats, but fidgeting on the spot (vibrating). A **liquid** is like a busy school corridor at changeover: people are close together and touching, but they can shuffle past one another and the crowd flows to fill the shape of the corridor. A **gas** is like students running around on a huge field at break: far apart, moving fast in random directions and colliding now and then. More energy (excitement) means more movement. Where it breaks down: people choose where to go, but particles move randomly; people tire and slow down, while particles keep moving unless energy is transferred away; and real particles are not big individual objects with gaps that look anything like the size of a crowd.

terms.d: A very small piece of matter, such as an atom or a molecule.
The model that matter is made of particles in constant motion, used to explain the states of matter.
The three forms of a substance: solid, liquid and gas.
A state with particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating about fixed positions; fixed shape and volume.
A state with particles close together but randomly arranged, able to move past each other; fixed volume, no fixed shape.
A state with particles far apart, moving quickly and randomly; no fixed shape or volume.
The regular, repeating arrangement of particles in a solid.
Move backwards and forwards about a fixed position.
The forces between particles that pull them together; strongest in solids, weakest in gases.
The energy an object has because it is moving.
A measure related to the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.
Able to be squashed into a smaller volume; true of gases because of the large gaps between particles.
A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.
Movement in unpredictable, constantly changing directions, caused by collisions between particles.
The spreading out and mixing of particles due to their random motion.
A change, such as a change of state, in which no new substance is made and the change can be reversed.

mistakes.w: Particles in a solid do not move.
mistakes.r: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions.

mistakes.w: Particles in a liquid are far apart.
mistakes.r: Particles in a liquid are close together (mostly touching) but randomly arranged.

mistakes.w: Gas particles get bigger when heated.
mistakes.r: The particles stay the same size; they move faster and (if free to) further apart.

mistakes.w: There is air between the particles of a gas.
mistakes.r: There is empty space (nothing) between the particles of a gas.

mistakes.w: Liquids can be compressed easily.
mistakes.r: Liquids are very hard to compress because their particles are already touching.

mistakes.w: A gas has a fixed volume.
mistakes.r: A gas has no fixed volume; it expands to fill its container.

mistakes.w: Solid particles are arranged randomly.
mistakes.r: Solid particles are arranged in a regular pattern.

mistakes.w: The particles melt when a solid melts.
mistakes.r: The particles stay the same; they gain energy and break free from fixed positions.

mistakes.w: Drawing liquid particles with large gaps or in neat rows.
mistakes.r: Draw liquid particles touching, randomly arranged, with no regular pattern.

exam.q: Describe the arrangement of particles in a solid.
model: Particles are close together / touching.
In a regular pattern / fixed arrangement.
exam.tip: Two separate ideas: spacing and pattern.

exam.q: Describe the movement of particles in a gas.
model: Move quickly / fast.
In random directions.
exam.tip: Speed and randomness both score.

exam.q: State which state of matter has particles with the most kinetic energy.
model: Gas.
exam.tip: For the same substance.

exam.q: Explain why a gas can be compressed but a liquid cannot.
model: Gas particles are far apart / large spaces between them, so they can be pushed closer together.
Liquid particles are already close together / touching, so there is no space to move into.
exam.tip: Compare both states.

exam.q: Explain why a liquid takes the shape of its container but a solid does not.
model: Particles in a liquid can move past each other / are not in fixed positions.
Particles in a solid are held in fixed positions by strong forces.
exam.tip: Mention movement AND forces.

exam.q: Draw particle diagrams to show the arrangement of particles in a liquid and in a gas.
model: Liquid: particles mostly touching, random arrangement, at least 5 particles.
Gas: particles widely spaced, random, not touching.
exam.tip: Equal-sized circles, never overlapping.

exam.q: Describe what happens to the particles in a block of ice as it is heated until it melts.
model: Particles gain (kinetic) energy.
They vibrate more / faster.
They overcome (some of) the forces holding them in fixed positions and can move past each other.
exam.tip: Energy, vibration, forces: three marks.

exam.q: Compare the forces between particles in solids, liquids and gases.
model: Strongest in solids, weaker in liquids.
Very weak / negligible in gases.
exam.tip: Use comparative words.

exam.q: Use the particle model to explain why a smell from a perfume spreads across a room.
model: Perfume particles (as a gas) move randomly / quickly.
They collide with air particles and change direction.
So they gradually spread out through the room (diffusion).
exam.tip: Random motion is the key idea.

exam.q: Use the kinetic theory to compare the properties of solids, liquids and gases. Your answer should refer to the arrangement, movement and energy of the particles.
model: Solid: particles close together in regular pattern; vibrate about fixed positions.
Solid: strong forces, so fixed shape and volume, cannot be compressed.
Liquid: particles close but random; can move past each other.
Liquid: fixed volume, flows, takes container shape, hard to compress.
Gas: particles far apart, moving quickly and randomly, very weak forces.
Gas: fills container, easily compressed; particles have most energy, solids least.
exam.tip: Structure your answer state by state and link each property to a particle reason.

exam.q: Give two limitations of using a particle diagram to represent a gas.
model: Diagram is 2D but particles are in 3D / particles not really solid spheres.
Spacing between gas particles is really much larger than shown / motion and forces are not shown.
exam.tip: Any two sensible limitations.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain, using the particle model, why a solid has a fixed shape.
steps: Identify arrangement: particles are close together in a regular pattern.
Identify forces: there are strong forces of attraction between particles.
Identify movement: particles can only vibrate about fixed positions.
Link to property: because particles cannot move past each other, the shape cannot change.
worked.ans: The particles in a solid are held in fixed positions by strong forces and can only vibrate, so they cannot move past each other and the solid keeps a fixed shape.

worked.q: Applied example: A syringe is filled with air and sealed. The plunger is pushed in. Then the syringe is filled with water and the test is repeated. Explain the results.
steps: Air: the plunger moves in easily.
Reason: air is a gas, so its particles are far apart with large empty spaces.
Pushing moves the particles closer together, so the volume decreases.
Reason: water is a liquid, so its particles are already close together / touching.
There is almost no space to push them into, so the liquid cannot be compressed.
worked.ans: Air is compressed because gas particles have large spaces between them; water is not because liquid particles are already touching.

worked.q: Model answer: Describe how the movement and energy of the particles change as water at 20 degrees C is heated to steam.
steps: At 20 degrees C (liquid): particles are close together and move past each other randomly.
As temperature rises, particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.
At boiling, particles gain enough energy to overcome the forces between them.
As steam (gas): particles are far apart, moving quickly in random directions with very weak forces between them.
worked.ans: The particles gain energy and move faster; on boiling they overcome the forces between them and become far apart, moving rapidly and randomly as a gas.

phy_edx.13.1.summary: **Density** tells you how much **mass** is packed into a given **volume** of a material. You must recall and use the equation **density = mass / volume (ρ = m / V)**, with density measured in **kg/m³** (or g/cm³). Dense materials such as lead have a lot of mass in a small volume, while materials such as polystyrene or air have little mass in a large volume. Being able to rearrange the equation, convert between units and calculate volumes of regular shapes lets you answer any density calculation in the exam.

core.p: Density is a property of a **material**, not of a particular object. It compares how much **mass** there is with how much **space (volume)** that mass takes up. A small lead fishing weight and a huge lead block have the **same density**, even though their masses are very different.
bullets: **High density**: a lot of mass in a small volume (for example lead, gold, iron).
**Low density**: a small mass spread over a large volume (for example cork, polystyrene, air).
Density does **not depend on the size** of the sample, only on what it is made of (and its state and temperature).
Cutting an object in half halves both mass and volume, so the density stays the same.

callouts.p: The mass per unit volume of a material.

core.p: You must be able to **recall and use** the density equation. The symbol for density is the Greek letter **rho (ρ)**, which looks like a curly p.
bullets: **density = mass / volume**
ρ = density in **kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³)**.
m = mass in **kilograms (kg)**.
V = volume in **cubic metres (m³)**.
If mass is in grams and volume in cm³, density comes out in **g/cm³**.

callouts.p: density (kg/m³) = mass (kg) / volume (m³); ρ = m / V
This equation is not given on the equation sheet: learn it by heart.

fig.cap: The density formula triangle: cover the quantity you want to find. Covering m leaves ρ x V; covering ρ leaves m over V; covering V leaves m over ρ.

core.p: Exam questions often give you density and ask for mass or volume. Rearrange **before** substituting, or substitute first and then rearrange: either way, show your working.
bullets: To find density: **ρ = m / V**.
To find mass: **m = ρ x V**.
To find volume: **V = m / ρ**.
Check the answer makes sense: a dense material should have a small volume for a given mass.

core.p: Density has two common units. The **SI unit** is **kg/m³**, but in the laboratory masses are measured in grams and volumes in cm³, giving **g/cm³**. You must be able to convert between them.
bullets: To convert **g/cm³ to kg/m³**: multiply by 1000.
To convert **kg/m³ to g/cm³**: divide by 1000.
Water has a density of about **1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³**.

callouts.p: Never divide grams by m³ or kg by cm³. Make sure mass and volume units match the density unit you want.

core.p: Volume conversions are the most common source of lost marks. Because volume is **three-dimensional**, the conversion factor is **cubed**.
bullets: cm³ to m³: **divide by 1 000 000** (or multiply by 10^-6).
m³ to cm³: multiply by 1 000 000.
**1 cm³ = 1 ml** and **1000 cm³ = 1 litre (1 dm³)**.
Mass: **1 kg = 1000 g**; g to kg divide by 1000.

callouts.p: Convert every quantity into kg and m³ (or g and cm³) before substituting, then you cannot mix them up.

core.h: Finding the volume of a regular solid
core.p: For a regular shape such as a cube or cuboid, measure the **length, width and height** with a ruler, then multiply. Density questions frequently ask you to work out the volume first.
bullets: Cuboid: **V = length x width x height**.
Cube of side s: **V = s x s x s**.
Measure dimensions with a ruler (mm precision) or vernier callipers for small objects.
Measure mass with a **top-pan balance**.
Irregular objects are measured by **displacement** of water (see core practical 14.3).

fig.cap: Finding the density of a regular block. The volume is length x width x height = 5 cm x 4 cm x 2 cm = 40 cm³. With a mass of 108 g, the density is 108 / 40 = 2.7 g/cm³ (2700 kg/m³), which matches aluminium.

core.p: You do not need to memorise these values, but knowing roughly how big densities are helps you **sense-check** answers. Notice that gases are around **a thousand times less dense** than solids and liquids.
bullets: Most metals: several thousand kg/m³.
Water: about 1000 kg/m³ (1 g/cm³).
Air at room temperature: about 1.2 kg/m³.
If your answer for a metal is 2.7 kg/m³, you have probably forgotten a unit conversion (2.7 g/cm³ = 2700 kg/m³).

core.p: Two objects can have the **same mass** but very different sizes. The denser material takes up **less space**. Equally, two objects of the **same volume** can have very different masses.
bullets: 1 kg of iron occupies about 127 cm³ (a cube about 5 cm across).
1 kg of wood (about 600 kg/m³) occupies about 1700 cm³ (a cube about 12 cm across).
Same volume: a 1 cm³ cube of gold has a mass of about 19 g, but a 1 cm³ cube of cork is only about 0.24 g.
So 'heavy' and 'dense' are not the same thing: a large log is heavier than a small iron nail but less dense.

callouts.p: Density compares mass to volume. A big object can be heavy but have a low density.

fig.cap: Two objects with the same mass of 1 kg. Iron is much denser than wood, so 1 kg of iron takes up a much smaller volume than 1 kg of wood.

core.p: Comparing densities lets you predict whether something will **float or sink**. An object (or a liquid that does not mix) that is **less dense** than the liquid it is placed in will float; one that is **more dense** will sink.
bullets: Ice (920 kg/m³) floats on water (1000 kg/m³).
Iron (7900 kg/m³) sinks in water but floats on mercury (13 600 kg/m³).
Oil is less dense than water, so it floats on top.
Ships float despite being steel because their hull contains a lot of air, so the **average density** of the ship is less than that of water.

core.h: Why different states have different densities (link)
core.p: Density links directly to the particle model. In **solids and liquids** particles are close together, so there is a lot of mass in each cubic metre. In **gases** the particles are far apart, so the density is much lower. This is explored further in 14.4-14.5.
bullets: Solids are usually slightly denser than their liquids (particles closer together).
Water is an exception: ice is **less dense** than liquid water, so ice floats.
A gas has a much lower density than the same substance as a liquid.
Compressing a gas into a smaller volume increases its density (same mass, smaller volume).

core.p: Follow the same five steps every time. Most density questions are 2 or 3 marks, and each step can earn credit.
bullets: 1. Write the equation: **ρ = m / V**.
2. Convert units so they match (kg and m³, or g and cm³).
3. Substitute the values.
4. Rearrange if needed and calculate.
5. Give the answer with the **correct unit** and sensible significant figures.
If you need volume first, calculate it from the dimensions before using the density equation.

callouts.p: Writing kg/m³ or g/cm³ after the answer is often required. Write the unit the question asks for.

analogy.p: Think of density as how **crowded** a lift is. The lift's size is the volume and the total mass of the people inside is the mass. A small lift packed with people is like a dense material such as lead: lots of mass in little space. A huge lift with three people is like polystyrene or a gas: little mass spread over a big space. Doubling the size of the lift and doubling the number of people keeps it just as crowded, just as a bigger lump of the same material has the same density. Where it breaks down: people are all roughly the same mass, but different atoms have very different masses, so a material can be dense because its atoms are heavy (like gold) as well as because they are closely packed.

terms.d: The mass per unit volume of a material; ρ = m / V.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg).
The amount of space an object takes up, measured in m³ or cm³.
The Greek letter used as the symbol for density.
The SI unit of density: kilograms per cubic metre.
A common laboratory unit of density; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
The SI unit of volume; the volume of a cube with 1 m sides; equal to 1 000 000 cm³.
The volume of a cube with 1 cm sides; equal to 1 ml.
An object with a simple shape (such as a cuboid) whose volume can be calculated from its measured dimensions.
An object whose volume cannot be calculated from its dimensions and is found by displacement of water.
Finding volume by measuring the volume of water pushed aside when an object is submerged.
An electronic balance used to measure mass.
The total mass of an object divided by its total volume, including any air spaces.
An object floats in a liquid if its average density is less than the density of the liquid.

mistakes.r: density = mass / volume (ρ = m / V).

mistakes.r: Convert so units match: kg with m³, or g with cm³.

mistakes.r: 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³ because 100 x 100 x 100.

mistakes.r: Multiply by 1000: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

mistakes.w: A bigger piece of the same metal has a bigger density.
mistakes.r: Density is a property of the material; it does not depend on the size of the sample.

mistakes.w: Heavy objects are dense.
mistakes.r: Density depends on mass AND volume; a large heavy object may have a low density.

mistakes.w: Giving density in kg or in m³.
mistakes.r: Density units are kg/m³ or g/cm³.

mistakes.r: m = ρ x V.

exam.q: Write down the equation that links density, mass and volume.
model: density = mass / volume (ρ = m / V).
exam.tip: Must be recalled.

exam.q: State the SI unit of density.
model: kg/m³ (kilograms per cubic metre).
exam.tip: g/cm³ is also a density unit but not SI.

exam.q: A block has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
model: = 2.7 g/cm³.
exam.tip: Units already match: no conversion needed.

exam.q: Convert a density of 7.9 g/cm³ into kg/m³.
model: 7900 kg/m³.
exam.tip: Multiply by 1000.

exam.q: A stone has a density of 2500 kg/m³ and a volume of 0.0040 m³. Calculate its mass.
model: m = ρ x V.
exam.tip: Rearrange first.

exam.q: The density of water is 1000 kg/m³. Calculate the volume of 3.0 kg of water.
model: V = m / ρ.
exam.tip: 0.0030 m³ = 3000 cm³ = 3 litres: sense check.

exam.q: A metal cuboid measures 2.0 cm x 3.0 cm x 5.0 cm and has a mass of 267 g. Calculate its density and suggest which metal it is (copper 8.9 g/cm³, iron 7.9 g/cm³, aluminium 2.7 g/cm³).
model: = 8.9 g/cm³.
Copper.
exam.tip: Find volume first, then density, then compare.

exam.q: A gold ring has a mass of 9.65 g. Gold has a density of 19 300 kg/m³. Calculate the volume of the ring in cm³.
model: Convert density: 19 300 kg/m³ = 19.3 g/cm³.
exam.tip: Convert density to g/cm³ to match grams.

exam.q: Explain why a large wooden log can have a greater mass than a small iron nail even though iron has a greater density.
model: Mass = density x volume.
The log has a much larger volume, so its mass can be larger despite its lower density.
exam.tip: Use the equation in your explanation.

exam.q: A student says 'if you cut a block of aluminium in half, each half has half the density'. Explain why the student is wrong.
model: Both the mass and the volume are halved.
So mass / volume (the density) stays the same.
exam.tip: Density is a property of the material.

exam.q: A tank of air of volume 0.050 m³ contains 0.060 kg of air. It is pumped up until it contains 0.30 kg of air in the same volume. Calculate the density of the air before and after, and explain the change.
model: Density increases by 5 times.
Because more mass (more particles) is packed into the same volume.
exam.tip: Same volume, more mass: higher density.

worked.q: A rectangular block of metal is 10 cm long, 5.0 cm wide and 2.0 cm high. Its mass is 0.79 kg. Calculate its density in kg/m³.
steps: Volume in cm³: V = 10 x 5.0 x 2.0 = 100 cm³.
worked.ans: ρ = 7900 kg/m³

worked.q: Olive oil has a density of 920 kg/m³. Calculate the mass of oil in a full 2.0 litre bottle.
A piece of cork has a mass of 6.0 g. Cork has a density of 0.24 g/cm³. Calculate its volume, and state whether it would float in water (1.0 g/cm³).
steps: Compare densities: 0.24 g/cm³ is less than 1.0 g/cm³.
So the cork is less dense than water and floats.
worked.ans: V = 25 cm³; it floats because it is less dense than water.

phy_edx.13.2.summary: In this core practical you find the **density** of a regular solid, an irregular solid and a liquid by measuring **mass** with a top-pan balance and **volume** by measuring dimensions, by **displacement** of water (eureka can or measuring cylinder) or directly with a measuring cylinder. You then use **density = mass / volume** (ρ = m / V). Grade 9 answers explain how to make each measurement accurate, how to reduce uncertainty, and how to convert units between g/cm³ and kg/m³.

core.h: Aim and the equation you use
core.p: The aim is to determine the density of solids and liquids. Density tells you how much mass is packed into each unit of volume. Every method in this practical is just a way of getting a reliable **mass** and a reliable **volume**, then dividing.
bullets: **density = mass / volume**, written ρ = m / V
ρ (rho) is density in **kg/m³** (or g/cm³ in the lab)
m is mass in **kg** (or g), measured with a **top-pan (electronic) balance**
V is volume in **m³** (or cm³); 1 ml = 1 cm³
Rearranged: m = ρ x V and V = m / ρ
The independent variable is the object or liquid tested; the dependent variable is the calculated density

callouts.p: Density is the mass per unit volume of a material: density = mass / volume.
ρ = m / V must be recalled and used; it is not always given on the equation sheet in the form you need, so learn all three arrangements.

fig.cap: The density formula triangle: cover the quantity you want. Cover m to get m = ρ x V; cover V to get V = m / ρ; cover ρ to get ρ = m / V.

core.p: Choose each piece of apparatus because of the measurement it makes and its resolution. A more precise instrument (smaller divisions) gives a smaller uncertainty.
bullets: **Top-pan balance** (resolution often 0.01 g or 0.1 g) to measure mass
**Ruler** (1 mm resolution) for large regular objects
**Vernier calipers** (0.1 mm) or **micrometer** (0.01 mm) for small regular objects
**Eureka can** (displacement can) with a spout, for irregular objects
**Measuring cylinder** (choose the smallest that holds the volume, for the finest scale)
Thread or cotton to lower the object gently; water; the liquid to be tested; paper towels

callouts.p: In a 2 mark question say which instrument AND why: for example vernier calipers because they have a higher resolution than a ruler, so the percentage uncertainty in a small length is smaller.

core.p: A regular solid (cube, cuboid, cylinder) has a shape whose volume you can calculate from its measured dimensions. This avoids water entirely.
bullets: Measure the **mass** of the object on a top-pan balance (zero it first)
Measure **length, width and height** with a ruler or vernier calipers
Repeat each length in **several places** and take a mean, in case the block is not perfectly square
Calculate volume: cuboid **V = length x width x height**; cylinder V = π r² h
Calculate density ρ = m / V
Keep units consistent: g with cm³ gives g/cm³

callouts.p: If you measure in mm, convert to cm (divide by 10) before multiplying, or your volume will be 1000 times too big in mm³ compared with cm³.

fig.cap: A regular cuboid. Measure its length, width and height (ideally with vernier calipers), multiply them to get the volume, then divide the mass by this volume.

core.h: Method 2: an irregular solid using a eureka can
core.p: An irregular object (a stone, a lump of plasticine, a key) has no simple formula for its volume, so you measure the volume of water it **displaces**. The object pushes aside exactly its own volume of water when fully submerged.
bullets: Measure the **mass** of the dry object on a balance
Fill the eureka can with water **above the spout** and let the excess drain until it stops dripping
Place an empty measuring cylinder under the spout
Lower the object **gently on a thread** until it is **fully submerged**
Collect all the displaced water; wait until dripping stops
Read the volume in the measuring cylinder at **eye level**, from the **bottom of the meniscus**: this equals the object's volume
Calculate ρ = m / V

callouts.p: Water cannot be compressed, so the volume of water that overflows equals the volume of the submerged object.
Measure the mass while the object is dry. A wet object has extra water on it, so its mass reading is too high.

core.h: Method 2b: an irregular solid in a measuring cylinder
core.p: If the object is small enough to fit inside a measuring cylinder you can use the cylinder alone. The rise in the water level equals the object's volume.
bullets: Half fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume V1
Tilt the cylinder and slide the object in (or lower it on a thread) so no water splashes out
Make sure the object is fully submerged and no air bubbles cling to it
Record the new volume V2
Volume of object **V = V2 - V1**
This is quicker but only works for objects that fit through the neck of the cylinder

core.p: For a liquid you measure the mass of a known volume. The trick is to remove the mass of the container, either by taring the balance or by subtracting.
bullets: Place an empty measuring cylinder on the balance and **zero (tare)** it, or record its mass m1
Pour in a measured volume of the liquid, for example 50 cm³, reading the **bottom of the meniscus at eye level**
Record the new mass m2; mass of liquid **m = m2 - m1** (or the reading directly if tared)
Calculate ρ = m / V
Repeat for different volumes (for example 10, 20 ... 50 cm³) and calculate a mean density, or plot mass against volume: the **gradient** is the density
Pure water should give about 1.0 g/cm³ (1000 kg/m³), a good check of your method

callouts.p: A graph of mass (y) against volume (x) should be a straight line through the origin. Its gradient = mass / volume = density, and using a gradient averages out random errors.

core.p: Most marks for this practical are about measuring carefully. Each technique below reduces a specific error.
bullets: Read a measuring cylinder with your eye **level with the meniscus** to avoid **parallax error**
Read the **bottom of the meniscus** for water and most liquids
**Zero the balance** before use to avoid a **zero error**
Use the **smallest measuring cylinder** that holds the volume, because it has finer graduations
Use **vernier calipers or a micrometer** rather than a ruler for small lengths
Lower objects on a thread so water does not **splash** out of the can or cylinder
Make sure the object is **fully submerged** and remove trapped **air bubbles**, which would add to the measured volume

callouts.p: An error in a reading caused by viewing a scale from an angle rather than at eye level, at right angles to the scale.

core.h: Sources of error and how to reduce them
core.p: Errors make your density too high or too low. In 6 mark questions you gain credit for linking each error to its effect on the result.
bullets: Water left on the object before weighing: mass too high, so **density too high**
Air bubbles on a submerged object: volume too large, so **density too low**
Eureka can not filled to the spout first: some displaced water is not collected, volume too small, **density too high**
Water drops left on the spout or in the cylinder: volume too small
Splashing when the object is dropped in: water lost, volume reading wrong
Object that absorbs water (wood, sponge) or floats: displacement does not give the true volume; a floating object must be pushed under with a thin pin
**Repeat** readings and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of **random errors**

callouts.p: Repeating and averaging reduces random errors. It does NOT remove a systematic error such as an unzeroed balance; that must be fixed by zeroing the instrument.

core.p: Lab measurements are usually in grams and cubic centimetres, but the SI unit of density is kg/m³. You must be able to convert confidently.
bullets: **1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³**
To convert g/cm³ to kg/m³: **multiply by 1000**
To convert kg/m³ to g/cm³: divide by 1000
1 ml = 1 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 0.001 m³
Water: 1.0 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³

callouts.p: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. A common exam step is to convert a lab answer in g/cm³ into kg/m³.

core.p: A grade 9 answer talks about how confident you can be in the result. The biggest percentage uncertainty usually comes from the smallest measurement.
bullets: **Resolution** is the smallest change an instrument can show
A small object displaces only a few cm³, so a 1 cm³ reading uncertainty can be a large **percentage uncertainty**
Improve by using a **larger sample** (or several identical objects at once) or a narrower measuring cylinder
**Repeatable**: the same person gets similar results with the same method
**Reproducible**: others get similar results with different equipment
Results are **precise** if repeat values are close together, and **accurate** if they are close to the true value

callouts.p: If asked how to improve accuracy for a small irregular object, say: use a measuring cylinder with a smaller scale division, or measure several identical objects together, to reduce the percentage uncertainty in volume.

core.p: This is a low hazard practical, but examiners can still ask for a sensible precaution.
bullets: Wipe up spilled water so nobody slips and to protect the balance
Keep water away from the mains-powered balance
Lower heavy objects on a thread so they do not crack the glass cylinder
Use a tray to catch overflow
Handle any liquid other than water (for example oil or salt solution) with care and wear eye protection if it is an irritant

core.p: Once you have a density, compare it with known values to identify the material or to judge the quality of the method.
bullets: Compare with a table of known densities to **identify the material**
Calculate a **mean** from repeats, ignoring any **anomalous** results
Percentage difference = (your value - accepted value) / accepted value x 100
Explain any difference using a specific error and its direction
An object with density greater than 1.0 g/cm³ sinks in water; less than 1.0 g/cm³ floats
State the answer to a sensible number of **significant figures** (no more than the data)

callouts.p: If your measurements are to 3 significant figures, give the density to 3 significant figures. Writing 2.7142857 g/cm³ shows false precision.

analogy.p: Density is like how tightly a suitcase is packed: mass is how heavy the contents are and volume is the size of the case. Two cases the same size can weigh very different amounts. In the practical, weighing the case is the balance and finding its size is either a tape measure (regular solid) or seeing how much water it pushes out of a full bath (displacement). The analogy breaks down because a suitcase can be squashed and has empty air inside, whereas the solid's volume is fixed and the material fills it all, and because real displacement only works if the object is fully under the water and does not soak any up.

terms.d: Mass per unit volume of a material; density = mass / volume.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kg or g with a balance.
The amount of space an object occupies, measured in m³ or cm³.
A solid with a simple shape whose volume can be calculated from measured dimensions.
A solid with no simple shape; its volume is found by displacement.
Pushing aside of a liquid by a submerged object; the volume displaced equals the object's volume.
A can with a spout used to collect the water displaced by an object.
A graduated cylinder used to measure the volume of a liquid.
The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow tube; read from the bottom for water.
An error caused by reading a scale from an angle instead of at eye level.
An electronic instrument that measures mass.
Setting a balance to read zero, often with a container on it, so only the added mass is measured.
A systematic error where an instrument does not read zero when it should.
The smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect.
An unpredictable variation in readings, reduced by repeating and taking a mean.
An error that shifts all readings by the same amount in the same direction.
An instrument that measures lengths to a resolution of 0.1 mm.

mistakes.w: Density = volume / mass
mistakes.r: Density = mass / volume (ρ = m / V).

mistakes.w: Read the top of the meniscus
mistakes.r: Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level to avoid parallax error.

mistakes.w: Drop the object into the eureka can
mistakes.r: Lower it gently on a thread to avoid splashing and losing water.

mistakes.w: Put the object in before filling the eureka can to the spout
mistakes.r: Fill above the spout and let it drain to the spout level first, so all displaced water is collected.

mistakes.w: 1 g/cm³ = 1 kg/m³
mistakes.r: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ (multiply by 1000).

mistakes.w: Repeating readings removes zero error
mistakes.r: Repeating reduces random error; a zero error is systematic and is removed by zeroing the balance.

mistakes.w: Weigh the object after it has been in the water
mistakes.r: Measure the mass while the object is dry, otherwise the mass is too high.

mistakes.w: Units of density are kg/m or kg x m³
mistakes.r: Units are kg/m³ (or g/cm³).

mistakes.w: Air bubbles make the density higher
mistakes.r: Air bubbles increase the measured volume, so the calculated density is too low.

exam.q: State the equation linking density, mass and volume.
model: density = mass / volume (ρ = m / V)
exam.tip: Words or symbols are both accepted; make sure mass is on top.

exam.q: Name the piece of apparatus used to measure the mass of a stone.
model: (Top-pan / electronic) balance
exam.tip: Do not write 'scales' alone in a higher mark answer; balance is the expected word.

exam.q: Describe how a student should read the volume of water in a measuring cylinder.
model: Eye level with the surface / meniscus (to avoid parallax)
Read from the bottom of the meniscus
exam.tip: Two separate ideas: where your eye is, and which part of the curve.

exam.q: Explain why the student should lower the stone into the eureka can on a thread rather than dropping it.
model: Dropping it causes splashing / water lost from the can
So the volume collected would not equal the volume of the stone (too small)
exam.tip: Always link the action to its effect on the measurement.

exam.q: A block of metal has mass 540 g and measures 5.0 cm x 4.0 cm x 10.0 cm. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
model: = 2.7 g/cm³
exam.tip: Show the volume calculation as a separate line to collect method marks.

exam.q: Convert 2.7 g/cm³ to kg/m³.
model: 2700 kg/m³
exam.tip: Multiply by 1000.

exam.q: A student found a volume of 12 cm³ for a stone using a measuring cylinder with 1 cm³ divisions. Suggest how she could make the volume measurement more precise.
model: Use a measuring cylinder with smaller divisions / higher resolution (narrower cylinder)
Or measure several identical stones at once, so percentage uncertainty is smaller
exam.tip: Precision is about resolution and percentage uncertainty.

exam.q: A student forgot to wait for the eureka can to stop dripping before placing the measuring cylinder under the spout. Explain the effect on the calculated density.
model: Extra water (not displaced by object) is collected
So the measured volume is too large
So the calculated density is too low
exam.tip: Chain: error, effect on V or m, effect on ρ.

exam.q: Describe how to determine the density of a liquid, such as cooking oil.
model: Place empty measuring cylinder on balance and zero / record its mass
Pour in a known volume of oil, read at eye level from the meniscus
Record the mass and subtract the mass of the cylinder
Calculate density = mass / volume (repeat and find a mean)
exam.tip: Include how the cylinder's mass is removed; it is the step most often missed.

exam.q: Describe a method to determine the density of an irregularly shaped stone. In your answer, explain how you would make your measurements as accurate as possible.
model: Measure mass of the dry stone on a zeroed top-pan balance
Fill a eureka can with water until it drips from the spout; wait until it stops
Place a measuring cylinder under the spout
Lower the stone on a thread until fully submerged, avoiding splashing
Read the volume of displaced water at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus
Volume of water = volume of stone; density = mass / volume
Repeat and calculate a mean; remove air bubbles; use smallest suitable measuring cylinder
exam.tip: Level 3 needs a logically ordered method and at least two accuracy points linked to why they help.

exam.q: A student plots a graph of mass against volume for a liquid. State what the gradient represents.
model: Density (of the liquid)
exam.tip: Gradient = change in y / change in x = mass / volume.

worked.q: A stone has a mass of 78.0 g. When lowered into a eureka can it displaces 30.0 cm³ of water. Calculate its density in g/cm³ and in kg/m³.
steps: Write the equation: ρ = m / V
worked.ans: 2.60 g/cm³ = 2600 kg/m³

worked.q: An empty measuring cylinder has a mass of 62.5 g. With 50.0 cm³ of salt water added, the total mass is 114.0 g. Calculate the density of the salt water.
worked.ans: 1.03 g/cm³ (1030 kg/m³)

worked.q: A cylinder of metal has diameter 2.0 cm, height 5.0 cm and mass 124 g. Calculate its density.
worked.ans: 7.9 g/cm³ (7900 kg/m³)

phy_edx.13.3.summary: The density of a substance depends on how closely its **particles** (atoms or molecules) are packed. Solids and liquids have particles **close together**, so they have high densities that are similar to each other, while gases have particles **far apart**, so their density is much lower. When a substance melts, freezes, evaporates, boils, condenses or sublimes, the **mass is conserved** because the number of particles does not change. These are **physical changes**: unlike chemical changes, the material **recovers its original properties** if the change is reversed.

core.p: Every substance is made of tiny particles. The mass of each particle stays the same whatever the state, so the density depends on **how many particles are packed into each cubic metre**. More particles per unit volume means more mass per unit volume, which means a higher density.
bullets: density = mass / volume (ρ = m / V)
Same particles in every state, so **mass per particle is unchanged**
Closer spacing means more particles in a given volume, so **higher density**
Wider spacing means fewer particles in a given volume, so **lower density**
Density differences between states are explained by **arrangement and spacing**, not by particles changing size
Particles themselves do **not** expand or shrink when heated

callouts.p: Density is high when particles are close together and low when they are far apart, because the same mass then fills a smaller or larger volume.

core.p: In a solid the particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction. They vibrate about these positions but cannot move past each other.
bullets: Particles **close together** (touching) in a **regular** pattern (lattice)
Particles **vibrate about fixed positions**
Strong forces between particles hold a **fixed shape** and **fixed volume**
Many particles per unit volume, so **high density**
Usually the **most dense** state of a substance

core.p: In a liquid the particles are still close together but are arranged randomly and can slide past one another. Because they are still touching, the volume hardly changes when a solid melts.
bullets: Particles **close together** but in a **random (irregular)** arrangement
Particles **move around and slide past each other**
Liquids flow and take the shape of their container but have a **fixed volume**
Spacing is only slightly greater than in a solid, so density is **similar to (usually slightly less than) the solid**
Liquids are almost incompressible because the particles are already touching

callouts.t: Why solid and liquid densities are close
callouts.p: Explain that in both states the particles are close together / touching, so the number of particles in a given volume is about the same.

core.p: In a gas the particles are far apart and move quickly in random directions. Most of a gas is empty space, which is why gases have such low densities.
bullets: Particles **far apart** with a **random** arrangement
Particles **move quickly in all directions**, colliding with each other and the container walls
Weak or negligible forces between particles
No fixed shape or volume: a gas **fills its container**
Very few particles per unit volume, so **much lower density** than solids and liquids (roughly 1000 times less)
Gases can be compressed because of the large spaces between particles

callouts.p: A gas has a much lower density than the same substance as a liquid or solid because its particles are much further apart, so the same mass takes up a much larger volume.

core.p: Use this table to compare states in one place. In 6 mark answers, compare arrangement, movement and spacing, then link spacing to density.
bullets: Solid to liquid: spacing changes a little, density changes a little
Liquid to gas: spacing increases hugely, density falls hugely
The mass of a sample is unchanged in each case

core.p: Real data show the pattern clearly: the solid and liquid forms of a substance have similar densities, while the gas is far less dense.
bullets: Water (liquid): about **1000 kg/m³**
Ice (solid water): about **920 kg/m³**
Steam at 100 °C: about **0.6 kg/m³**
Air at room temperature: about **1.2 kg/m³**
Iron (solid): about 7900 kg/m³

callouts.p: For most substances the solid is denser than the liquid, but ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats. Do not use water as your example of the general rule.

core.p: A change of state happens when energy is transferred to or from a substance, changing how the particles are arranged and how they move. You need to name all six changes.
bullets: **Melting**: solid to liquid
**Freezing**: liquid to solid
**Evaporating**: liquid to gas, at the surface, at any temperature
**Boiling**: liquid to gas, throughout the liquid, at the boiling point
**Condensing**: gas to liquid
**Sublimating (sublimation)**: solid directly to gas, for example solid carbon dioxide (dry ice)
Heating (energy in) causes melting, boiling, evaporating and sublimating; cooling (energy out) causes freezing and condensing

core.h: Conservation of mass in changes of state
core.p: When a substance changes state, its particles are rearranged and move differently, but **no particles are created or destroyed**. Since each particle keeps its mass, the total mass stays exactly the same.
bullets: Mass is conserved when substances **melt, freeze, evaporate, boil, condense or sublimate**
The **number of particles** stays the same; only their spacing, arrangement and motion change
Volume can change a lot (especially liquid to gas), but **mass does not**
So density changes in a change of state because **volume** changes, not mass
Example: 1 kg of ice melts to give 1 kg of water

callouts.p: When a substance changes state, mass is conserved because the number of particles stays the same.

core.h: Why open containers seem to lose mass
core.p: If you heat water in an open beaker, the balance reading falls. This does not break conservation of mass: the water particles have simply left the beaker as vapour.
bullets: Evaporation or boiling in an **open** container lets gas particles **escape** into the air
The mass of the beaker and contents falls, but the **total mass** of water (liquid plus vapour) is unchanged
To demonstrate conservation, use a **sealed (closed) container**
Similarly, condensation on a cold can adds mass because water vapour from the air turns to liquid on it

callouts.p: Do not say mass is destroyed when water boils. Say the water vapour escapes from the open container, so the measured mass decreases.

core.p: Changes of state are **physical changes**. The particles themselves are not changed, only rearranged, so reversing the change gives back the original material with all its original properties.
bullets: In a physical change **no new substance** is formed
The material **recovers its original properties** if the change is reversed (ice melted then refrozen is still ice)
In a **chemical change** the atoms rearrange to form **new substances** with different properties (for example burning, rusting)
Chemical changes are usually hard to reverse
Mass is conserved in both, but only a physical change gives back the original substance on reversing

callouts.p: A change in which no new substance is formed and the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.

core.p: Because mass is fixed, any change in volume during a change of state produces a change in density. Use ρ = m / V to reason about this.
bullets: Liquid to gas: volume increases enormously, so **density falls** enormously
Gas to liquid (condensing): volume decreases, density rises
Solid to liquid: volume usually increases slightly, so density falls slightly
Water freezing is unusual: volume **increases**, so ice is **less dense** and floats; this is why pipes can burst in winter
If mass is constant, density and volume are inversely proportional

callouts.p: State the arrangement in each state, describe spacing, link spacing to particles per unit volume, then to density. Finish with mass conserved because the number of particles is unchanged.

analogy.p: Imagine the particles are pupils. In assembly (solid) they sit in neat rows, packed close. At break in the corridor (liquid) they are still shoulder to shoulder but jostle and move past each other, so the same number fit in nearly the same space. On the playing field (gas) they spread far apart and run around, so the same number of pupils now fill a huge area: low density. However many times they move between assembly, corridor and field, the number of pupils (the mass) is the same. The analogy breaks down because pupils choose where to go, whereas particles change state only when energy is transferred, and real particles are identical while pupils are not.

terms.d: Mass per unit volume: density = mass / volume.
A tiny piece of matter, such as an atom or molecule.
The model that all matter is made of tiny particles whose arrangement and motion explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.
State with particles close together in a regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions.
State with particles close together in a random arrangement, able to move past each other.
State with particles far apart, moving quickly and randomly.
Change of state from solid to liquid.
Change of state from liquid to solid.
Change from liquid to gas at the surface of a liquid, at temperatures below the boiling point.
Change from liquid to gas throughout the liquid, at the boiling point.
Change of state from gas to liquid.
Change of state directly from solid to gas.
The total mass stays the same during a change, because no particles are created or destroyed.
A change where no new substance forms and the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.
A change in which new substances with different properties are formed.
A system in which no matter can enter or leave, so the total mass is constant.

mistakes.w: Particles get bigger when a solid melts or a liquid boils
mistakes.r: The particles stay the same size; the spaces between them change.

mistakes.w: Gases are less dense because their particles are lighter
mistakes.r: Gas particles have the same mass as in the liquid; they are further apart, so there are fewer per unit volume.

mistakes.w: Mass decreases when water boils
mistakes.r: Mass is conserved; in an open container the vapour escapes, so the measured mass falls, but no mass is destroyed.

mistakes.w: Liquids are much less dense than solids
mistakes.r: Liquid and solid densities are similar because particles are close together in both.

mistakes.w: Particles in a solid do not move
mistakes.r: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions.

mistakes.w: Melting is a chemical change
mistakes.r: Changes of state are physical changes: no new substance is formed and the change can be reversed.

mistakes.w: Sublimation is a gas turning into a liquid
mistakes.r: Sublimation is a solid turning directly into a gas.

mistakes.w: Evaporation and boiling are the same
mistakes.r: Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

mistakes.w: Ice floats because it is lighter
mistakes.r: Ice floats because it is less dense than water (less mass per unit volume).

exam.q: Name the change of state when a solid turns directly into a gas.
model: Sublimation / sublimating
exam.tip: Spell it carefully; 'sublimination' may not be accepted.

exam.q: State what happens to the mass of a block of ice as it melts.
model: It stays the same / is conserved
exam.tip: One word answers like 'same' are fine.

exam.q: Explain why mass is conserved when water evaporates in a sealed container.
model: The number of particles / molecules stays the same
No particles can enter or leave the sealed container (particles are only rearranged)
exam.tip: Mention particles; 'nothing is lost' alone may not score.

exam.q: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a liquid.
model: Close together in a random / irregular arrangement
Move around / slide past each other
exam.tip: One mark for arrangement, one for movement.

exam.q: Explain why the density of a gas is much lower than the density of the same substance as a liquid.
model: Particles in a gas are much further apart
So the same mass occupies a much larger volume / fewer particles per unit volume
exam.tip: Link spacing to volume or particles per unit volume; do not say particles are lighter.

exam.q: Explain why the density of a solid is similar to the density of the same substance as a liquid.
model: In both, the particles are close together / touching
So the number of particles per unit volume is similar
exam.tip: Comparison questions need both states mentioned.

exam.q: State two differences between a physical change and a chemical change.
model: Physical change: no new substance formed (chemical: new substance formed)
Physical change is reversible and the material recovers its original properties (chemical: not easily reversed)
exam.tip: Make each point a comparison.

exam.q: A student heats 200 g of water in an open beaker. After 10 minutes the balance reads 185 g. Explain this result.
model: Some water evaporated / boiled to form water vapour
The vapour escaped from the open beaker, so mass is still conserved overall (15 g of water left as gas)
exam.tip: Show you still believe in conservation of mass.

exam.q: Ice has a density of 920 kg/m³. Water has a density of 1000 kg/m³. Explain why water pipes can burst when the water in them freezes.
model: Mass of water stays the same when it freezes
Ice has a lower density so it has a larger volume (V = m / ρ)
Ice expands and pushes on the pipe walls, causing it to burst
exam.tip: Use density = mass / volume with constant mass.

exam.q: Use the particle model to explain the differences in density between solids, liquids and gases.
model: Solid: particles close together in a regular arrangement, vibrate about fixed positions
Liquid: particles close together, random arrangement, can move past each other
Gas: particles far apart, random, move quickly
Density = mass / volume; mass of each particle unchanged
Solids and liquids: many particles per unit volume, so high and similar densities
Gas: few particles per unit volume, so a much lower density
exam.tip: Level 3 needs all three states AND the link from spacing to density.

worked.q: A 0.50 kg block of ice (density 920 kg/m³) melts completely. Water has a density of 1000 kg/m³. Calculate the volume of the ice and the volume of the water formed.
steps: Mass is conserved, so the water also has a mass of 0.50 kg
Volume of ice: V = m / ρ = 0.50 / 920 = 0.000543 m³
The volume decreases on melting, so water is denser than ice
worked.ans: Ice 5.4 x 10⁻⁴ m³; water 5.0 x 10⁻⁴ m³

worked.q: 1.0 kg of water (density 1000 kg/m³) is boiled to form steam with density 0.60 kg/m³. Calculate how many times larger the volume of the steam is.
steps: Mass is conserved: steam mass = 1.0 kg
worked.ans: The steam occupies about 1700 times the volume of the water.

worked.q: A student puts 20 g of solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) into a sealed bag on a balance. Describe and explain what happens to the reading as the dry ice sublimes.
steps: Dry ice changes directly from solid to gas (sublimation)
The bag inflates because the gas particles are much further apart, so the volume increases
No particles enter or leave the sealed bag
So the number of particles, and therefore the mass, is unchanged
worked.ans: The reading stays at 20 g (plus the bag) because mass is conserved in a change of state.

phy_edx.13.4.summary: Heating a system transfers energy to its **thermal energy store**, increasing the **internal energy** of its particles. This either **raises the temperature** (particles gain kinetic energy) or **changes the state** (particles gain potential energy as forces between them are overcome), with the temperature staying constant during the change of state. **Specific heat capacity** is the energy to raise 1 kg by 1 °C, used in **ΔQ = m x c x Δθ**, and **specific latent heat** is the energy to change the state of 1 kg without a temperature change, used in **Q = m x L**.

core.p: When you heat a substance you transfer energy to it. That energy is stored by its particles as **internal energy**. What the energy does depends on whether the substance is changing state at the time.
bullets: Heating **increases the energy stored** within the system (its thermal energy store)
**Internal energy** = total **kinetic energy** + **potential energy** of all the particles
If the energy increases the **kinetic energy** of particles, the **temperature rises**
If the energy increases the **potential energy** of particles (overcoming forces between them), the substance **changes state**
During a change of state the **temperature stays constant** even though energy is still being supplied
Cooling a system does the reverse: internal energy falls, temperature falls or the substance condenses or freezes

callouts.p: The total energy stored by the particles in a system: the sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles.
Heating a system either raises its temperature or produces a change of state.

core.h: Temperature is not the same as energy
core.p: Temperature measures the **average kinetic energy** of the particles, not the total energy. A bath of warm water stores far more energy than a cup of boiling water because it has many more particles.
bullets: Temperature is measured in **°C** (or K) with a thermometer
Energy is measured in **joules (J)**
A larger mass at the same temperature stores **more** internal energy
Two objects at the same temperature can store different amounts of energy
Energy is transferred by heating from a **hotter** to a **colder** object

callouts.p: Do not use 'heat' and 'temperature' as if they mean the same thing. Energy transferred is in J; temperature is in °C.

core.p: If you heat a solid at a steady rate and plot temperature against time, you get a graph with **sloping sections** (temperature rising) and **flat sections** (changes of state).
bullets: **Sloping** section: energy increases particle **kinetic energy**, so temperature rises
**Flat** section at the **melting point**: solid and liquid present, energy breaks bonds / overcomes forces
**Flat** section at the **boiling point**: liquid and gas present
The boiling plateau is usually **longer** than the melting plateau because far more energy is needed to separate particles completely (L for vaporisation is larger than L for fusion)
A cooling curve has flat sections at the same temperatures, where energy is **released** as the substance condenses or freezes
The **gradient** of a sloping section depends on the specific heat capacity of that state and the heating rate

callouts.p: If asked why the temperature stays constant, say energy is being used to break bonds / overcome forces between particles (increasing potential energy), not to increase kinetic energy.

core.p: Different materials need different amounts of energy to warm up by the same amount. **Specific heat capacity** measures this. Water has a very high value, which is why it is used in radiators and why the sea warms slowly.
bullets: Symbol **c**, unit **J/kg °C** (joules per kilogram per degree Celsius)
Water: c = **4200 J/kg °C**
A **high c** material needs a lot of energy to heat up and releases a lot when it cools: it warms and cools slowly
A **low c** material (for example copper) heats up quickly for a given energy input
Used when the temperature changes and there is **no change of state**

callouts.p: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.

core.h: Using ΔQ = m x c x Δθ
core.p: This equation gives the energy needed to change the temperature of a mass of material. It is on the Edexcel equation sheet, but you must be able to select it, rearrange it and use the right units.
bullets: **change in thermal energy (J) = mass (kg) x specific heat capacity (J/kg °C) x change in temperature (°C)**
ΔQ = m x c x Δθ
Δθ = **final temperature - initial temperature**
Rearranged: c = ΔQ / (m x Δθ); m = ΔQ / (c x Δθ); Δθ = ΔQ / (m x c)
Convert grams to kg (divide by 1000) and kJ to J (multiply by 1000)
A temperature change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K, so Δθ is the same in either unit

callouts.p: Δθ is the change in temperature, not the final temperature. Heating water from 20 °C to 80 °C gives Δθ = 60 °C.

core.p: During a change of state the temperature does not change, so ΔQ = m c Δθ cannot be used. Instead we use **specific latent heat**, the energy needed per kilogram to change state.
bullets: Symbol **L**, unit **J/kg**
'Latent' means hidden: the energy goes in but no temperature rise is seen
The energy increases the **potential energy** of particles (breaking bonds / overcoming forces) rather than kinetic energy
The same amount of energy is **released** when the substance changes back (freezing or condensing)
The value depends on the substance and on which change of state it is

callouts.p: The energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without a change in temperature.

core.p: There are two specific latent heats for each substance, one for each pair of state changes.
bullets: **Specific latent heat of fusion**: energy to change 1 kg from **solid to liquid** (melting) at constant temperature; same energy released on freezing
**Specific latent heat of vaporisation**: energy to change 1 kg from **liquid to gas** (boiling) at constant temperature; same energy released on condensing
For water: L fusion = **334 000 J/kg**, L vaporisation = **2 260 000 J/kg**
Vaporisation needs much more energy because particles must be separated **completely** and pushed far apart, rather than just loosened

callouts.p: Steam at 100 °C causes worse burns than water at 100 °C because it releases its latent heat of vaporisation as it condenses on the skin, before cooling further.

core.p: This equation gives the thermal energy needed for a change of state. It is on the equation sheet; choose the correct L for the change described.
bullets: **thermal energy for a change of state (J) = mass (kg) x specific latent heat (J/kg)**
Q = m x L
Rearranged: L = Q / m; m = Q / L
There is **no temperature** in this equation: the temperature is constant during the change
Use L of fusion for melting or freezing, L of vaporisation for boiling or condensing

callouts.p: To take ice at 0 °C to water at 20 °C: first Q = m L (melting), then ΔQ = m c Δθ (warming). Add the two energies.

core.h: Specific heat capacity versus specific latent heat
core.p: The spec asks you to explain the difference between the two. The key is whether the temperature changes.
bullets: Specific heat capacity: **temperature changes**, no change of state, energy raises particle **kinetic** energy
Specific latent heat: **state changes**, no temperature change, energy raises particle **potential** energy
SHC unit J/kg °C has a temperature part; SLH unit J/kg does not
Both are energy **per kilogram**, so both depend on the material, not the amount
