phy_edx.13.9.summary: When a force compresses a gas, for example when a bicycle pump handle is pushed in, **work is done on the gas**. Work done is energy transferred, so the **internal energy** of the gas increases: the particles bounce off the inward-moving piston faster, their **average kinetic energy increases**, and so the **temperature of the gas rises**. This is why a bicycle pump gets warm, and the reverse effect (a gas doing work as it expands) explains why an aerosol can feels cold.

core.p: In physics, **work is done** when a force moves an object a distance in the direction of the force. Doing work always **transfers energy**. When you push a piston into a gas, you exert a force over a distance, so you do work on the gas and transfer energy to it.
bullets: **Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force**, E = F × d.
Work done is measured in **joules (J)**; 1 J = 1 N m.
Work done on a system = energy transferred to that system.
For a gas, the energy goes into the **internal energy** of the gas (mainly the kinetic energy of its particles).

callouts.p: Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance.

core.p: The **internal energy** of a system is the total energy stored by its particles: the sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles. In a gas, the forces between particles are tiny, so internal energy is mostly the **kinetic energy** of the moving particles.
bullets: Increasing the internal energy of a gas mainly increases the kinetic energy of its particles.
Temperature is a measure of the **average kinetic energy** of the particles.
So increasing the kinetic energy of gas particles **increases the temperature**.
Internal energy can be increased by **heating** the gas or by **doing work** on it.

callouts.p: You can raise the temperature of a gas by heating it or by doing work on it (compressing it). Both transfer energy to the particles.

core.h: Why compressing a gas raises its temperature
core.p: This is the core explanation for 14.20P. Write it as a chain of linked steps.
bullets: A force pushes the piston inwards, compressing the gas.
**Work is done on the gas** by the force (force × distance).
This transfers energy to the gas, increasing its **internal energy**.
The **kinetic energy of the particles increases**, so they move faster on average.
Because temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles, the **temperature of the gas increases**.

callouts.p: Work done on gas → energy transferred → internal energy increases → particles' kinetic energy increases → temperature increases.

core.h: Particle picture: bouncing off a moving piston
core.p: At the level of individual particles, the speed increase happens because the piston is **moving towards** the particles when they hit it.
bullets: A particle hits the inward-moving piston and rebounds.
Because the piston is moving towards it, the particle rebounds with a **greater speed** than it arrived with, like a tennis ball hit by a racket moving forwards.
The piston has done work on the particle, giving it more kinetic energy.
Many particles gain speed this way, so the average kinetic energy and temperature of the gas rise.
If the piston is stationary, particles rebound at the same speed, so no work is done and no temperature rise occurs from this effect.

core.p: The bicycle pump is the example the spec names. When you pump up a tyre, the barrel of the pump, especially near the end where the air leaves, becomes noticeably **warm**.
bullets: Pushing the handle pushes the piston into the barrel, compressing the air.
You exert a force over a distance, so **you do work on the air**.
Energy is transferred to the air, increasing its internal energy.
The air particles move faster, so the air's **temperature rises**.
Energy is then transferred by heating from the hot air to the **barrel** of the pump, which feels warm.
Pumping repeatedly and quickly makes the pump hotter because work is done faster than energy can escape to the surroundings.

callouts.p: Some heating is from friction between piston and barrel, but the exam wants the main reason: work done on the gas increases its internal energy and temperature.

core.p: How quickly the gas is compressed affects how much its temperature rises.
bullets: **Fast compression**: work is done quickly, so there is little time for energy to transfer to the surroundings; the temperature rises noticeably.
**Slow compression**: energy has time to transfer by heating to the surroundings, so the temperature can stay nearly constant.
This is why pV = constant experiments are done slowly: to keep temperature constant.
In fast compression, pressure rises for two reasons: smaller volume (more frequent collisions) and higher temperature (faster particles hitting harder).

head: Compression
Energy lost to surroundings
Temperature change
Pressure rise
rows: Greater: volume and temperature both cause it

core.h: The reverse: a gas doing work as it expands
core.p: If a gas expands and pushes something outwards, **the gas does work** on its surroundings. Energy is transferred out of the gas, so its internal energy and temperature **decrease**.
bullets: When gas pushes a piston outwards, particles rebound from the receding piston more slowly.
The kinetic energy of the particles decreases, so the temperature falls.
Example: gas sprayed from an **aerosol can** expands rapidly and the can and spray feel cold.
Example: a carbon dioxide fire extinguisher nozzle becomes very cold during use.
Example: letting air out of a tyre valve quickly, the escaping air feels cool.

callouts.p: Work done ON the gas: temperature rises. Work done BY the gas: temperature falls.

core.p: Using the idea in different contexts shows full understanding.
bullets: **Diesel engines**: air is compressed very rapidly in the cylinder, heating it enough to ignite the fuel without a spark plug.
**Bicycle and football pumps** get warm during use.
**Refrigerators and heat pumps** use compression (heating the gas) and expansion (cooling the gas) of a refrigerant to move energy.
**Spacecraft re-entry**: air in front of the craft is compressed rapidly, causing very high temperatures.
**Scuba tank filling**: tanks become warm as air is compressed into them, so they are often filled in cool water.

core.p: Doing work on a gas obeys the principle of conservation of energy: energy is not created, only transferred between stores.
bullets: Your muscles' chemical energy store is transferred mechanically by the force on the piston.
The energy ends up in the internal (thermal) energy store of the gas.
Some is then dissipated by heating to the pump barrel and the surroundings.
The total energy before equals the total energy after.

callouts.p: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.

core.p: Extended questions often ask you to explain the temperature rise in a pump or engine and link it to pressure.
bullets: Start with the force and distance: **work is done on the gas**.
State that this **transfers energy** to the gas and **increases its internal energy**.
Explain that the particles gain **kinetic energy** and move faster.
Conclude that the **temperature increases** (temperature relates to average kinetic energy).
If asked about pressure, add that faster particles in a smaller volume collide with the walls more often and with more force.
Finish by linking to the observation (warm pump barrel, ignition in a diesel engine).

callouts.p: Credit-worthy words: work done, energy transferred, internal energy, kinetic energy of particles, temperature increases.

analogy.t: Tennis ball and a moving racket
analogy.p: A tennis ball bouncing off a wall that is still comes back at the same speed. But if you swing a racket towards the ball, it flies off much faster, because the racket did work on it. The inward-moving piston in a pump is like the swinging racket: every gas particle that hits it rebounds faster, so the gas particles gain kinetic energy and the gas gets hotter. If the racket moves away as the ball hits (a gas expanding), the ball comes off slower, like a gas cooling as it expands. Where it breaks down: a racket hits one ball, but the piston hits billions of particles that move randomly in all directions and then share their energy through collisions with each other.

terms.d: Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance; work done = force × distance.
The unit of energy and of work done; 1 J is the work done by a force of 1 N moving 1 m.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
Energy an object has because it is moving; for gas particles it increases with temperature.
A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.
Reducing the volume of a gas by pushing on it, which involves doing work on the gas.
Increasing the volume of a gas; an expanding gas does work on its surroundings and cools.
A sliding part in a cylinder that can compress or be pushed by a gas.
A cylinder and piston that compresses air to push it into a tyre; it gets warm as work is done on the air.
The energy store associated with the temperature of a substance.
Energy transferred to the surroundings, usually by heating, that is not useful.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores.
Energy transfer because of a temperature difference.
An engine in which rapid compression heats air enough to ignite the fuel.

mistakes.w: The pump gets hot only because of friction.
mistakes.r: Work is done on the gas, increasing its internal energy and the kinetic energy of its particles, so the gas temperature rises (friction is a minor effect).

mistakes.w: Compressing the gas makes the particles collide more, which creates heat.
mistakes.r: Work done on the gas transfers energy to it, so the particles' kinetic energy increases and temperature rises.

mistakes.w: The particles get hotter.
mistakes.r: Individual particles move faster (gain kinetic energy); temperature is a property of the whole gas.

mistakes.w: Doing work on the gas increases the potential energy of the particles.
mistakes.r: It mainly increases the kinetic energy of the particles.

mistakes.w: Temperature increases because the particles are squashed closer together.
mistakes.r: Temperature rises because particles gain kinetic energy from the work done; being closer together does not by itself raise temperature.

mistakes.w: An expanding gas gets hotter because there is more space.
mistakes.r: An expanding gas does work on its surroundings, so it loses internal energy and its temperature falls.

mistakes.w: Work done on a gas is the same as heating it with a flame.
mistakes.r: Both increase internal energy, but work done is a mechanical transfer (force over a distance), not heating.

mistakes.w: Missing out the energy step: 'the piston pushes so the temperature goes up'.
mistakes.r: State that work done transfers energy to the gas, increasing its internal energy.

exam.q: State what happens to the temperature of a gas when work is done on it by compressing it quickly.
model: It increases
exam.tip: One-word answers are fine for one mark.

exam.q: State what is meant by the internal energy of a gas.
model: Total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles (in the gas)
exam.tip: Include both kinetic and potential, and 'all the particles'.

exam.q: State the equation linking work done, force and distance moved.
model: work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force
exam.tip: Include 'in the direction of the force' for precision.

exam.q: When a bicycle pump is used, the barrel of the pump gets warm. Explain why.
model: Work is done on the air (gas) when it is compressed
The internal energy / kinetic energy of the air particles increases
So the temperature of the air rises and energy is transferred to the barrel by heating
exam.tip: Start from 'work is done on the gas'.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of particles, why a gas gets hotter when a piston is pushed into it.
model: Particles hit the piston as it moves inwards
Particles rebound with a greater speed / gain kinetic energy
Average kinetic energy increases so temperature increases
exam.tip: Link average kinetic energy to temperature.

exam.q: Explain why an aerosol can becomes cold when the gas is released quickly.
model: The gas expands and does work on the surroundings
The internal energy / kinetic energy of the particles decreases so temperature falls
exam.tip: This is the reverse of doing work on a gas.

exam.q: A force of 60 N pushes a pump piston a distance of 0.30 m. Calculate the work done on the gas.
model: Work done = 60 × 0.30
exam.tip: Distance must be in metres.

exam.q: Explain why the temperature of a gas rises more when it is compressed quickly than when it is compressed slowly.
model: Quick compression: less time for energy to be transferred to the surroundings
So more of the energy from the work done stays as internal energy of the gas, raising temperature more
exam.tip: Slow compression lets energy escape, keeping temperature nearly constant.

exam.q: In a diesel engine, air is compressed rapidly in a cylinder until it is hot enough to ignite fuel. Explain how the compression increases the temperature of the air.
model: Piston does work on the air
Work done transfers energy to the air / internal energy increases
Kinetic energy of the air particles increases / particles move faster
Temperature increases (rapid compression means little energy lost)
exam.tip: Four marks: four linked steps.

exam.q: A student uses a bicycle pump to inflate a tyre and notices the pump gets warm. Explain why this happens and describe what happens to the pressure of the air in the pump while the handle is pushed in. Use ideas about particles and energy.
model: Pushing the handle exerts a force over a distance so work is done on the air
Energy is transferred to the air, increasing its internal energy
Air particles gain kinetic energy and move faster
So the temperature of the air increases; energy transfers to the barrel by heating so it feels warm
Volume decreases so particles collide with the walls more frequently
Faster particles also collide with more force, so the pressure increases
exam.tip: Cover both parts: the energy chain for temperature, and collisions for pressure.

worked.q: A student pushes a bicycle pump handle with an average force of 120 N through a distance of 0.25 m. Assuming all the work done goes into the internal energy of the air, how much does the internal energy increase?
steps: By conservation of energy, this energy is transferred to the air.
worked.ans: The internal energy of the air increases by 30 J (in reality slightly less, as some energy is dissipated by friction and heating the barrel).

worked.q: Explain why a football gets warm when it is pumped up quickly, and why it cools down again afterwards.
steps: Pumping quickly does work on the air, transferring energy to it.
The internal energy and the kinetic energy of the air particles increase, so the air temperature rises.
The warm air heats the ball's surface, so the ball feels warm.
Afterwards the warm ball transfers energy by heating to the cooler surroundings until it reaches room temperature.
worked.ans: Work done on the air raises its temperature; later, energy is dissipated to the surroundings so the ball cools to room temperature.

worked.q: Compare what happens to the gas temperature when a piston is pushed into a cylinder and when the gas pushes the piston out.
steps: Piston pushed in: work is done ON the gas; particles rebound faster from the moving piston.
Internal energy increases, so temperature rises.
Gas pushes piston out: work is done BY the gas; particles rebound more slowly from the receding piston.
Internal energy decreases, so temperature falls.
worked.ans: Compression (work done on the gas) heats it; expansion (work done by the gas) cools it.

svg.cap: The chain of reasoning for why doing work on a gas increases its temperature: work done transfers energy, the particles gain kinetic energy, the internal energy rises and so the temperature rises.
